sources.title: Nikos Kazantzakis (Q214622), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-18): English label 'Nikos Kazantzakis', description 'Greek writer, poet and philosopher (1883-1957)', instance of human, born 18 February 1883 (Julian date; 2 March Gregorian), died 26 October 1957, citizen of Greece, Korean label 니코스 카잔차키스. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

'Nikos Kazantzakis', Encyclopedia of World Biography (Gale; Encyclopedia.com reproduction, read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: calls him the foremost figure in modern Greek literature; law at Athens, philosophy in Paris, early plays and novels under pseudonyms; the Nietzsche pilgrimage and the years of inner struggle in Vienna and Berlin; the Odyssey: A Modern Sequel begun in 1924, rewritten seven times and published in December 1938; travel books from the 1920s; the occupation years on Aegina (Zorba the Greek, the Prometheus trilogy, a translation of the Iliad); the 1945-46 spell as minister and the self-exile that followed; Christ Recrucified (The Greek Passion), Freedom or Death, The Last Temptation of Christ (1951) and St. Francis of Assisi; the 1954 Vatican edict against the Last Temptation and his telegram of appeal; Report to Greco; the epitaph he asked for. Chronological reference entry, largely drawn from Helen Kazantzakis's biography of her husband, so admiring and partly spouse-sourced.

Peter Bien, 'Kazantzakis's abortive foray into politics in liberated Athens, 1944-46', Kampos: Cambridge Papers in Modern Greek no. 13 (2005; PDF read in full). Scholarly article by his leading English translator and biographer, drawing on letters, Helen Kazantzakis's biography, memoirs and an unpublished diary: his literary soirees and patience with young writers, his unsuccessful candidacy for the Academy of Athens (fifteen of thirty votes), his Nobel Prize campaign and the shared candidacy with Angelos Sikelianos, the forty days in Crete verifying German atrocities, the Socialist Workers' Union he led, his 46 days as minister without portfolio and his readiness to resign ('I feel terribly free'), the withdrawn production of his play Kapodistrias, detractors' view that he withdrew when he could not lead, and his return to solitude. Sympathetic but candid about contradictions; politics here is context, not scored.

N. Georgopoulos, 'Marxism and Kazantzakis', Byzantine and Modern Greek Studies vol. 3 (1977), pp. 175-200 (Cambridge Core; only the opening extract and the reference notes were readable, the full article is paywalled). Scholarly framing of the controversy around him: royalist governments attacked him as immoral and a Bolshevik, he was arrested in Crete in 1924 and accused in 1928 of being a Russian agent, while the Greek Communist Party refused him as bourgeois and decadent; a note records his December 1953 letter complaining that Greeks were bombarding the Swedish Academy with letters against him. Used only for those documented points.

John Sanidopoulos, 'The Myth of the Excommunication of Nikos Kazantzakis', Orthodox blog post, 31 January 2014 (read in full). Counter-voice from an Orthodox perspective that quotes scholarship (Charitini Christodoulou, Peter Bien 1989, Michalis Stafylas, Patroclos Stavrou): the 1930 charge of atheism after Saviors of God with a trial date set but never held, the Holy Synod's 1954 encyclical against Captain Michalis and The Last Temptation, a campaign for his excommunication that failed when Metropolitan Irineos asked whether his accusers had read the books and the Patriarchate declined to ratify it, and his telegram answering the Church. Argues he was never excommunicated; a blog, so used only for the documented episodes.

Michael Scott Joseph, 'The Odyssey by Nikos Kazantzakis', EBSCO Research Starters (2021; read in full). Research-starter summary of the 33,333-line epic Odysseia (1938): Odysseus leaves home after Troy, joins revolts in Crete and Egypt, founds and loses an ideal city, and makes a final journey south toward an iceberg in the Antarctic, ending in a mystical farewell to life; lists the main scholarship (Bien, Dombrowski, Levitt, Prevelakis). Used for the content and standing of the poem, not for behaviour.

Nick Trakakis, 'Greek literary figures: Nikos Kazantzakis', Neos Kosmos, 19 August 2010 (read in full). Short profile by a Monash University philosopher: the Nietzsche doctorate that the University of Athens rejected, the Bergson lectures in Paris, forty days on Mount Athos with Angelos Sikelianos, press assignments to Spain, England, Italy (including an interview with Mussolini), Russia, Egypt, Palestine and Japan, the charge of atheism after Saviors of God, the Odyssey after eight drafts, and the Last Temptation placed on the Vatican's Index and condemned by the Orthodox Synod. Gives 1885 as his birth year, which conflicts with Wikidata, the Gale entry and other sources (1883); used only for episodes not in dispute.

persistence.rationale: [src_kazantzakis_gale, src_kazantzakis_neoskosmos, src_kazantzakis_bien | 1924-1953 | reference entry, profile, scholarly article] The Odyssey was begun in 1924, rewritten seven times (eight drafts in one account) and published in 1938; during the occupation he kept producing work (Bien lists Zorba, the Iliad and Dante translations and several plays for 1940-44) and he finished St. Francis of Assisi in 1953 in poor health (Gale).

perfectionism.rationale: [src_kazantzakis_gale, src_kazantzakis_neoskosmos | 1938-1950 | reference entry, profile] Besides the seven or eight drafts of the Odyssey, the Gale entry says that after finishing Christ Recrucified in September 1948 he did a full rewrite by December 'as was his custom', gives a second rewrite of Freedom or Death, and mentions rewriting of the play Constantine Palaiologos. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.50 to 62 / 0.44 (strong_inference to inference) because the rewrite habit is stated by one chronology drawn from his wife's biography and the draft count differs between sources.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_kazantzakis_neoskosmos, src_kazantzakis_sanidopoulos, src_kazantzakis_gale, src_kazantzakis_bien, src_kazantzakis_georgopoulos | 1909-1955 | profile, blog quoting scholarship, reference entry, scholarly article] His Nietzsche doctorate was rejected in Athens, he was charged with atheism after Saviors of God, the Synod campaigned against his novels and the Vatican listed The Last Temptation, and both the royalist right and the Communist Party refused him; Bien says he resisted a narrow concept of political commitment all his life and quotes his 1947 view that the correct middle road had been lost.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_kazantzakis_gale, src_kazantzakis_neoskosmos, src_kazantzakis_bien | 1906-1955 | reference entry, profile, scholarly article] Work spanned novels, verse epic, plays, philosophical treatises, travel books, a history of Russian literature, translations of Dante and Homer, journalism, a screenplay and a ministerial post; Bien's list for his 1945 Academy candidacy adds translations from five languages. Almost all of it lies within writing and ideas, which keeps the score moderate.

autonomy_need.rationale: [src_kazantzakis_bien, src_kazantzakis_gale, src_kazantzakis_neoskosmos | 1927-1948 | scholarly article, reference entry, profile] He settled on Aegina in 1927 to arrange his travel writings and returned to the island for the occupation years, resigned as minister after 46 days saying he felt 'terribly free', returned to 'boundless solitude, his true climate' (Bien), and went into self-exile in France in 1946-48 believing his country had denied him (Gale); detractors told Bien he would not take a subordinate position. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 72 / 0.54 to 68 / 0.50 because Bien reads the resignation as relief at a goal achieved plus frustration, and the self-exile account is the Gale entry's paraphrase of his own belief.

achievement_drive.rationale: [src_kazantzakis_bien, src_kazantzakis_georgopoulos, src_kazantzakis_gale | 1945-1953 | scholarly article, scholarly article extract, reference entry] Bien writes that he wanted the Nobel Prize desperately, left no stone unturned in contacting influential people, and submitted an Academy candidacy in March 1945 backed by a long bibliography; a 1953 letter complains of Greek letters sent against him to the Swedish Academy. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.52 to 66 / 0.46 (strong_inference to inference) because the Nobel campaign is documented by one scholar and the second source is a footnote in an article read only in extract.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_kazantzakis_gale, src_kazantzakis_sanidopoulos, src_kazantzakis_bien, src_kazantzakis_georgopoulos | 1924-1955 | reference entry, blog quoting scholarship, scholarly article, scholarly article extract] He answered the Vatican edict with a telegram appealing to God's tribunal and answered the Synod with an ironic blessing, stayed in Athens through the press campaign and a general's threat after Kapodistrias, and kept publishing while charged with atheism and arrested in 1924; Bien also reports detractors saying he withdrew at the first setback. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.50 to 62 / 0.46 because his repeated retreats to solitude (Bien's own account) cut against tolerance, and his replies to the Church are largely quoted from his telegrams.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_kazantzakis_bien | 1944-1946 | scholarly article] Bien documents plans for a United States Institute of Greek Culture, an arts organisation drawn up with Karolos Koun and Emmanuel Hourmouzios (from a colleague's diary) and the Saturday soirees that grew into a party; none of the cultural projects materialised and the party was, in Bien's words, forced upon him by events. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 60 / 0.46 to 58 / 0.42 because the plans were largely proposed by governments and none came to anything, and Bien says the party was forced on him.

collaboration.rationale: [src_kazantzakis_bien, src_kazantzakis_gale | 1943-1946 | scholarly article, reference entry] He worked with the philologist Ioannis Kakridis on a translation of the Iliad, agreed with Angelos Sikelianos to seek the Nobel Prize jointly, and listened to young writers' work 'with the same patience and goodwill'; Gale describes his wife as his secretary and companion. Detractors in Bien describe him as unwilling to serve under others.

READ (6 sources besides Wikidata): Gale Encyclopedia of World Biography entry (full), Bien 2005 Kampos article (full PDF), Georgopoulos 1977 (opening extract and reference notes only; full text paywalled), Sanidopoulos 2014 post (full), EBSCO Research Starter on the Odyssey (full), Neos Kosmos 2010 profile (full). Not opened: Helen Kazantzakis's biography (the Gale entry and Bien rest heavily on it), Bien's two-volume biography, Prevelakis, Report to Greco and his letters (self-report not scored), Britannica (bot-walled, 403). Wikipedia and other wiki-style encyclopedias not used. INDEPENDENT BEHAVIOURAL FAMILIES: about 3 (Helen Kazantzakis lineage as carried by the Gale entry and echoed by Neos Kosmos; Bien's scholarly reading of the 1944-46 years with letters and a colleague's diary; the Church-controversy tradition in Sanidopoulos and Georgopoulos); the spouse's biography underlies much of the rest, so confidence is capped. ATTRIBUTION: attributable (extensive published work and scholarship). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Gale Encyclopedia of World Biography entry (https://www.encyclopedia.com/history/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/nikos-kazantzakis). ROWS: 9 scored; 5 lowered in self-calibration (perfectionism, autonomy need, achievement drive, conflict tolerance, proactive agency) for single-chronology concentration, contradictory evidence (his retreats, Bien's reading of the resignation) and events that forced his hand; pre-calibration scores are saved in the scratch notes; no raise flags. Sparse and moderate by design; no extreme scores. MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT GATE: PASS on all six checks (cards: the Odyssey epic, the postwar novels including Zorba and The Last Temptation, Saviors of God). CAVEATS: Gale says seven rewrites of the Odyssey, Neos Kosmos eight drafts (the card says seven); excommunication is disputed and the Orthodox post argues it never happened, so no card states it as fact; the Nobel loss by one vote and his burial are not cards because they are not in the sources read.
